                                      PROJECT NO. 58481
 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §       PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION §                     §
 STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                    §                     OF TEXAS


              TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS’ COMMENTS

                                      I.    INTRODUCTION

       Texas Industrial Energy Consumers (TIEC) appreciates Commission Staff’s (Staff’s)
efforts to incorporate stakeholder feedback into a Discussion Draft that provides a clear, uniform
interconnection process and financial obligations for large load customers. Essentially, the
Discussion Draft creates a three-step interconnection process with interim agreements and
financial requirements before a large load customer executes a final facilities extension agreement
(FEA): (1) initial interconnection request with disclosures and a study fee of $114,000 for loads
with requested peak demand between 75MW and 250MW, or $314,000 for loads greater than
250MW; (2) discretionary services agreement (DSA) with the applicable utility and a $/MW
security equal to $50,000 per MW; and (3) an “intermediate agreement” within 180 days after the
Large Load Interconnection Study, but before the large load is included in ERCOT’s planning
studies, with a financial security and a contribution in aid of construction (CIAC). Generally, the
Discussion Draft provides a helpful framework to solicit constructive feedback on each step. TIEC
generally agrees with this approach, but there are still a number of areas in the Discussion Draft
that should be further refined.

       Importantly, this rulemaking should be limited to the issues required to implement Senate
Bill (SB) 6. SB 6 provided explicit requirements around financial obligations, disclosures, and
curtailment during certain specified emergency scenarios.         SB 6 did not amend or expand
ERCOT’s general authority under PURA § 39.151, and nothing in SB 6 or existing law authorizes
ERCOT to establish or enforce new operational standards for pure retail customers that are not
participating in the wholesale market. As explained below, TIEC has serious concerns about the
propriety and legality of authorizing ERCOT to impose operational requirements on pure retail
customers. Moreover, with no limitations on what ERCOT may propose, TIEC is also concerned
about the potential feasibility, cost, and operational impacts on affected retail customers. For these


                                                  1
 reasons, the Commission should remove this proposed subsection and allow the elements of the
rule required by SB 6 to move forward.

       As TIEC noted in previous comments, TIEC members are predominantly high load factor
customers that pay tens or even hundreds of millions per year in transmission costs. These
businesses are also cost-sensitive. Having substantial amounts of cash and credit tied up for years
in the utility planning process can impede expansions in Texas, even when those amounts will
ultimately be refunded or applied toward a project. Accordingly, TIEC advocates for a balanced
framework that discourages speculative load forecasts without relying exclusively on a “pay to
play” mechanism to determine the legitimacy or viability of proposed projects. With this context,
TIEC recommends further refining the Discussion Draft as follows:

       (1)     Rename the “intermediate agreement” an “interconnection agreement,” or
               clarify the distinction. As a preliminary matter, TIEC reads the Discussion Draft’s
               version of “intermediate agreement” to be the same as a final FEA or services
               agreement today. Using the term “intermediate” indicates that another agreement
               will follow, but the Discussion Draft does not specify how this is meant to work.
               TIEC recommends renaming the “intermediate agreement” as an “interconnection
               agreement” to avoid confusion or, alternatively, clarifying how the intermediate
               agreement would interact with a final interconnection agreement.

       (2)     Redefine the CIAC and financial security requirements under the
               intermediate agreement. The costs covered by CIAC and financial security
               should be restructured to prevent cost-shifting without imposing an undue financial
               burden on businesses seeking to site in Texas. CIAC covers the costs of facilities
               that will be dedicated to the interconnecting large load customer. Additional
               financial security should cover the costs of utility system upgrades that will be
               needed to serve the large load customer plus other existing or pending customers.
               As discussed at the workshop by TIEC and multiple utilities, this will protect other
               customers against stranded costs without requiring individual large load customers
               to pay the full cost of facilities that will be used to serve the grid at large. The
               CIACs should also be trued-up for actual costs, as they are today.

       (3)     Specify that financial security under a subsequent, more mature agreement
               supersedes prior requirements. The financial obligation under an intermediate
               agreement should be based on the utility’s expected actual costs. To the extent
               prior agreements included a “proxy” for these costs, or required up-front funding
               of a subset of the costs (which is common under discretionary service agreements),
               these amounts should be applied toward the intermediate agreement and if the costs
               under the intermediate agreement are lower, this should supersede prior financial
               obligations. Once a utility and its ratepayers are protected from the expected costs
               of any build-out, additional security obligations will only deter business
               development by tying up cash or credit in the utility planning process.

                                                2
 (4)   For a withdrawn or canceled project, refund any remaining CIAC once all
      actual utility costs are covered. As noted above, the goal of this rulemaking (and
      SB 6) is to avoid stranded or shifted costs. The rule states that the CIAC is not
      refundable if a project is withdrawn or canceled, which will operate as an
      unnecessary penalty if a project is in its very early stage. If a project is withdrawn,
      only the actual utility expenditures should be covered by drawing on financial
      security and the CIAC, and any remaining balance should be refunded to the
      customer.

(5)   Clarify the disclosure for project developers to address scenarios where an
      affiliate pursues an interconnection for a known customer. As TIEC noted in
      previous comments, understanding whether an interconnection request is being
      pursued by a developer or on behalf of a known end-use customer may be valuable
      in refining future forecasts. TIEC anticipates there will be a higher execution rate
      and more fidelity to the information provided during the interconnection process
      when the end-use customer is known. For these reasons, TIEC generally supports
      including this disclosure in the rule. However, it is common for industrial
      companies to use an internal service affiliate to develop interconnections before
      transferring them to the end use customer. For example, a centralized land
      procurement entity is common for oil and gas companies, and often this entity
      secures the interconnection before transferring it to the specific operator. TIEC
      recommends refinements to capture this in the rule language.

(7)   Reduce the generic $/MW security and only apply the security to the
      incremental capacity for site expansions. Setting the $/MW security required
      under the DSA to $50,000/MW for the total site of both new and expanded
      interconnection requests risks creating a deterrent for economic activity. Instead,
      the Commission should consider lowering the security amount to $20,000/MW and
      only applying the security to the new, incremental capacity for expansions.
      Notably, the DSA security is just a placeholder security meant to help validate load
      prior to ERCOT and the interconnecting utility executing a more permanent
      agreement. Therefore, it does not need to be so high, and it does not need to apply
      to the existing capacity of a site. This could be a significant cost for traditional
      industrial companies pursuing multiple new sites each year. Alternatively, a
      bifurcated approach could be used for “extra” large load at 250 MW and above to
      lessen adverse impacts to traditional industrial companies developing multiple sites
      each year.

(8)   Waive the minimum study fee for studying an alternative site if the utility
      provides a long interconnection timeline. When there is a three or more year
      interconnection timeline, customers should be able to evaluate an alternative site
      without paying another minimum charge. The Commission should consider adding
      language to the Discussion Draft allowing customers to either cancel their request
      if service cannot be provided in less than three years and receive a refund of any
      unused study fees, or elect to study a different interconnection point by paying the
      actual study costs without a minimum fee.


                                        3
            (9)    Give utilities flexibility to work with customers in reallocating capacity. The
                  discussion draft requires utilities to reallocate costs if a large load customer misses
                  a milestone by eighteen months. While TIEC understands and appreciates the
                  desire to make unused capacity available to the system, the reality is that business
                  plans can change or be delayed by forces outside a customer’s control. The utilities
                  need to be able to consider this on a case-by-case basis. TIEC agrees with allowing
                  the utility to reallocate capacity after a specific period, but there may be instances
                  where it is more efficient to update the customer’s expected load ramp instead of
                  having the customer start over in the interconnection process due to a delay.

           These recommendations are addressed in general order of priority for TIEC, and are
discussed further below. A complete redline of TIEC’s recommended changes is also attached for
reference.

     II.     COMMENTS ON PROPOSED SUBSECTION (L), ALLOWING ERCOT TO
                       REGULATE PURE RETAIL CUSTOMERS

A.         The Commission should remove the proposed language that would give ERCOT carte
           blanche authority to impose operational requirements on large loads.
           Section (l) of the Discussion Draft adds controversial language allowing ERCOT to
establish operational standards for large load customers and requiring large load customers to
comply with ERCOT’s standards as a condition for interconnection and continued operations.
This is outside the scope of SB 6, legally controversial, and poor public policy. TIEC recommends
removing this from the rule.

           SB 6 did not amend or expand ERCOT’s general authority under PURA § 39.151, and
nothing in the existing statute authorizes ERCOT to establish or enforce new operational standards
for pure retail customers. Under SB 6, even the new curtailment requirements during emergency
conditions are to be implemented by the utility—not ERCOT. 1 As drafted, the language in the
Discussion Draft will subject existing traditional industrial facilities to ERCOT’s jurisdiction any



1
  PURA § 37.0561 (e) (“...After the independent organization deploys all available market services, except for
frequency responsive services, the independent organization may direct the applicable electric utility or municipally
owned utility to require the large load customer to either deploy the customer’s on-site backup generating facilities
or curtail load.”) (emphasis added); PURA § 39.170(a) (“The commission shall require the independent organization
certified under Section 39.151 for the ERCOT power region to ensure that each electric cooperative, transmission
and distribution utility, and municipally owned utility serving a transmission-voltage customer develops a protocol,
including the installation of any necessary equipment or technology before the customer is interconnected, to allow
the load to be curtailed during firm load shed. The electric cooperative, transmission and distribution utility, or
municipally owned utility shall confer with the customer to the extent feasible to shed load in a coordinated
manner.") (emphasis added).

                                                         4
 time a customer expands its interconnection beyond the 75 MW threshold. Moreover, the language
is essentially unlimited, lacking any meaningful restrictions or standards for ERCOT’s authority.
Essentially, the language would give ERCOT free rein to control all large loads, even though they
are not regulated entities or Market Participants. Critically, pure retail customers—regardless of
their size—are not staffed, trained, or positioned to understand and comply with ISO requirements.
These customers are typically not in the electricity business and asking them to have dedicated
personnel to track, understand, and implement RTO requirements would be extremely burdensome
and unprecedented. The grid and its reliability requirements exist to serve customers, not vice
versa. This novel, legally unsupported proposal would inevitably cause adverse financial and legal
ramifications for both existing and prospective businesses across Texas. This does not send the
signal that Texas is “open for business.”

       Instead, utilities can include interconnection specifications and requirements for customer
facilities in their tariffs or interconnection agreements. Customers have a direct relationship with
their utility and are accustomed to reviewing and complying with utility tariffs and standards.
Clear, upfront requirements for interconnection standards and facility specifications are familiar
for businesses—direct, unfettered regulation by the RTO is not.

       i.      ERCOT does not have the technical expertise to regulate large loads and has
               no incentive to facilitate business growth. Utilities are in a better position to
               impose technical specifications on customer interconnections, as they have
               always done.
       ERCOT does not directly interact with pure retail loads, and lacks the necessary expertise
to understand how loads in a wide variety of businesses operate their facilities. In contrast, utilities
routinely hire engineers and account representatives that have precisely this expertise. Notably,
industrial loads are not monolithic and have different operating characteristics, safety
requirements, and business needs. Impeding the operations of industrial facilities can create a risk
of equipment damage and longer-term load outages, along with creating health and safety risks for
industrial sites. For example, when ERCOT put forward NPRR1191, ERCOT suggested a uniform
approach for voltage ride-through and ramp-rate requirements without considering the impact the
requirements would have on the broader industrial community and without any evidence that
different types of large loads could even meet the requirements ERCOT attempted to impose. If
industrial facilities had been required to meet ERCOT’s proposed standards, it would have caused


                                                   5
 major damage to large synchronous motors at many sites, and it would have created health and
safety risks for site personnel and the general public. 2

        Further, unlike the utilities, ERCOT does not have the incentive to facilitate growth or
work collaboratively with business customers. Large industrial and manufacturing facilities invest
billions of dollars in Texas each year. ERCOT’s requirements for large load customers would
subject new and existing facilities to additional compliance costs for simply consuming power
from the grid. This is unprecedented and will be a substantial deterrent to industrial companies
looking to do business in ERCOT. These businesses will have to set up a compliance group to
monitor, attempt to influence, and manage RTO requirements in order to operate here. Depending
on the ultimate breadth and costs of ERCOT’s proposed requirements, this would not only be a
disincentive to locating a facility in ERCOT but could also cause existing facilities to seek to
relocate to more favorable jurisdictions.

        TIEC and others have repeatedly suggested that utilities are better positioned to work
directly with their customers to develop interconnection standards that address ERCOT’s
reliability concerns. Utilities have direct relationships with the loads, better insight into their
operations, more expertise, and the right incentives to balance reliability needs with supporting
economic growth. Utilities already have interconnection requirements and design specifications
for industrial facilities. 3 Some of these are tariff-based, but some are internal design specifications
that are not tariffed but are provided to large users. Industrial users are accustomed to working
with their utility to ensure that their equipment aligns with the utility’s specifications to ensure
reliability both for the grid and for their industrial facilities. This typically occurs as part of the
initial interconnection process or when the customer is pursuing an expansion, or occasionally as
changes occur on the utility’s system. While the requirements themselves need to be feasible and
appropriate, it may be possible to work with the utilities to come up with specifications that would
be more feasible and tailored for the industrial community and to implement this through the
utilities’ tariffs or other design requirements instead of requiring customers to create a direct

 relationship with ERCOT. Using the utilities’ tariffs or other design requirements also maintains
a clear line of responsibility for grid reliability and avoids creating conflicts between ERCOT’s
requirements and the design specifications imposed by the utilities. Additionally, ancillary
services may also help fill any operational gaps. These are known, familiar tools that do not create
the legal or policy issues associated with directly regulating retail customers.

        ii.      Legal challenges regarding ERCOT’s authority to regulate pure retail
                 customers could delay or impede SB 6 implementation.
        Importantly, PURA provides no legal authority to subject large load customers to
ERCOT’s regulations.          As discussed previously, and in contrast to the portions of PURA
addressing the utilities’ authority over retail customers, PURA lacks any provision providing
ERCOT direct, regulatory authority over retail customers. In fact, when the Legislature authorized
the Commission to certify an independent organization to establish and enforce reliability and
accountability procedures (i.e., ERCOT), the Legislature explicitly and exhaustively listed the
entities that were subject to the ERCOT protocols and other binding documents in PURA
§ 39.151(j). 4 The language has remained unchanged and still applies today:

                           (j) A retail electric provider, municipally owned utility,
                  electric cooperative, power marketer, transmission and distribution
                  utility, or power generation company shall observe all scheduling,
                  operating, planning, reliability, and settlement policies, rules,
                  guidelines, and procedures established by the independent system
                  operator in ERCOT. Failure to comply with this subsection may
                  result in the revocation, suspension, or amendment of a certificate
                  as provided by Section 39.356 or in the imposition of an
                  administrative penalty as provided by Section 39.357.

        Critically, PURA does not require retail customers to observe any of ERCOT’s rules.
Under fundamental statutory construction canons, the express mention of one thing excludes
anything not mentioned. 5 As a result, this is an exhaustive list of the entities that must comply


4
  Tex. S.B. 7, 76th Leg., Reg. Sess. (1999) (enrolled version), .(available at:
https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/76R/billtext/html/SB00007F.htm).
5
  See Conoco Phillips Co. v. Koopmann, 547 S.W.3d 858, 876–77 (Tex. 2018).

                                                         7
 with ERCOT requirements, other than entities who voluntarily submit to ERCOT’s requirements
as Market Participants in exchange for the privilege of participating in the wholesale market or
providing compensated services.            As PURA § 39.151(j) indicates, retail customers are not
wholesale market participants or regulated entities; they are not required to obtain any “certificate”
or registration from the Commission that may be revoked or suspended.                             Unlike Market
Participants who must agree to comply with and be bound by all ERCOT Protocols as a condition
of participating in the wholesale market, pure retail loads have made no such commitment and
have no such obligation. 6

         The Legislature would need to authorize ERCOT to regulate customers directly. PURA as
a whole is designed to provide reliable service to retail customers—not to regulate them. If
ERCOT is able to regulate large customers in this manner, it would create a harmful precedent that
could be expanded to other customer classes as well. Under this theory, there is nothing to restrict
ERCOT from regulating other activities that might affect reliability, such as residential AC usage.
Further evidence of the Legislature’s intent to limit ERCOT’s authority over retail customers is
contained in PURA § 39.151. When this section was adopted, which established ERCOT, the
Legislature specifically restricted ERCOT from imposing requirements on industrial generation
facilities (typically cogeneration) that would adversely affect or impede any associated retail
manufacturing or other internal process, except to the minimum extent necessary to maintain
reliability. 7   The point of this protection was to prevent ERCOT from indirectly imposing
requirements that affect retail customers by using on-site generation as the pretense. This
protection would be rendered meaningless if ERCOT can suddenly regulate retail customers
directly without restriction. Similarly, it would not make sense for ERCOT to have more
operational control over pure retail customers than associated industrial generating facilities under
PURA § 39.151(l). 8 Clearly, the legislature never envisioned regulating plain retail customers.

8
  Unlike the language in the rulemaking, PURA § 39.151(l) only permits ERCOT cannot impose operational
requirements that may adversely affect or impede any manufacturing or other internal process operation associated
with an industrial generation facility, except to the minimum extent necessary to assure reliability of the
transmission network. Essentially, ERCOT should consider all other options of addressing a reliability issue prior to
imposing an obligation on industrial generation facilities.

                                                         8
          As further evidence of this, during the 88th Session, the Legislature explicitly considered
allowing ERCOT to regulate all large loads, but rejected this concept. Initially, Senate Bill
(SB) 1929 (88R) proposed new language that would have given ERCOT authority to register and
impose requirements on all large loads. 9 However, after testimony and conversations, the bill
authors understood the imprudence of requiring large manufacturing loads to be subject to ERCOT
requirements, and limited the bill’s application. 10 When the bill ultimately passed, it was tightly
bracketed to only allow the Commission to register cryptocurrency facilities and provide the
Commission with certain information. 11 This legislative history further demonstrates that the
Legislature only intended to get information from virtual currency mining facilities and did not
support allowing ERCOT to impose operational requirements on all loads.

         Finally, ERCOT’s general mandate to ensure reliability under PURA § 39.151(a)(2) does
not trump the specific statutory statements in PURA § 39.151(j). Under Texas’ Code Construction
Act, when a statute conflicts, the more specific provision controls over a general provision.12
There are exceptions when the general provision is enacted after the specific provision, but
critically, the language around ERCOT’s general mandate (in PURA § 39.151(a)(2)) was added in
the same act as the language discussing which entities are subject to ERCOT’s rules and
regulations (in PURA § 39.151(j)). If the Legislature intended to allow ERCOT to regulate pure
retail customers, it would have listed retail customers in PURA § 39.151(j) and added language
directly addressing (and likely restricting) this authority. Interpreting ERCOT’s general mandate
as authority to impose requirements on any entity that may have an impact on grid reliability would

 lead to absurd results. For example, residential HVAC usage presents one of the single largest
reliability challenges from the load side, but ERCOT has no authority to tell homeowners what
type of air conditioning units to buy, or what the temperature settings must be in their homes.
Similarly, the Commission cannot bypass the restrictions on ERCOT’s authority in PURA §
39.151(j) in a rulemaking to authorize ERCOT to impose regulations on pure customers.

       iii.    At a minimum, this issue should be severed in a separate dedicated rulemaking
               to consider appropriate standards and limitations for this authority.
       As these comments illustrate, whether ERCOT has authority to impose operational
requirements on loads is a controversial issue that will have significant ramifications. Rather than
including this issue in the SB 6 rulemaking process, which needs to be expeditiously completed,
the Commission should sever it into a separate dedicated project if the Commission wishes to
consider it further. This would allow stakeholders to appropriately direct resources to consider
standards and limitations around this proposed authority.

       As noted above, ERCOT initially attempted to impose operational requirements on loads
in 2023 through NPRR 1191, and it does not appear that ERCOT has further vetted or considered
alternative approaches since then, such as working with utilities to get more information, adjusting
tariff requirements, creating a new ancillary service, etc. To the extent that the Commission
believes there are specific reliability issues that may necessitate imposing new requirements on
retail loads, a separate rulemaking on the issue would allow for a more robust legal analysis and
provide a greater opportunity for entities to engage in the discussion and help the Commission and
ERCOT fully consider the potential implications and alternative solutions.

       III.   COMMENTS ON SECTIONS OF THE RULE IMPLEMENTING SB 6

A.     The “intermediate agreement” should be renamed, or the rule should clarify the
       distinction between the intermediate agreement and a final interconnection
       agreement/FEA.
       As a preliminary matter, the Discussion Draft contemplates large load customers entering
into an “intermediate agreement” after the interconnecting utility and ERCOT complete the large
load interconnection study. However, this “intermediate agreement” appears to meet all the
requirements for a final FEA. Given this, TIEC suggests renaming the “intermediate agreement”
as an “interconnection agreement.” This rulemaking is meant to provide consistency across
utilities, and it would be helpful for their customers if utilities used the same nomenclature for the

                                                 10
 agreements during each stage of the interconnection process. Notably, renaming the intermediate
agreement should not impact whether the utility can capture additional information that is not
contemplated in this rulemaking in its interconnection agreement. Consistent with this approach,
TIEC recommends changing all references throughout the Discussion Draft from the “intermediate
agreement” to the “interconnection agreement” and has included this in the attached complete
redline. Alternatively, the rule should clarify how the intermediate agreement relates to a final
FEA.

B.      The CIAC and financial security obligations should be refined to ensure appropriate
        cost assignment of customer-dedicated versus grid-dedicated facilities.
        The structure of the CIAC and the financial security in Sections (h)(8) and (h)(9) of the
Discussion Draft would require large customers to pay for facilities that will be used to serve other
customers and the grid at large. This is discriminatory compared to how smaller customers are
treated and will deter economic development in Texas. The goal of the rule should be to protect
other customers against stranded costs or cost-shifting, but not to require large load customers to
pay for more than their fair share of grid costs.

        Generally, a CIAC is a non-refundable payment equal to the cost of customer-dedicated
facilities, while financial security also includes collateral or credit that can be drawn upon to
protect ratepayers from the costs of system-wide upgrades if the customer’s project is canceled.
As Oncor described in its comments in Project No. 58484, the Commission should distinguish
between interconnection costs for facilities that are dedicated to the customer (included in the
CIAC) and transmission system upgrade costs for all customers (included in the financial security)
based on who “could” use the facilities. 13 The transmission grid is not static. It will change with
time, and by defining these categories of facilities based on potential use, the Commission can
create a clear line of demarcation that applies ERCOT-wide and across the lifespan of transmission
assets. As Oncor noted, Oncor’s west Texas transmission system grew one radial customer
extension after another, and lines that were initially meant to serve one customer now serve the
entire transmission system. 14 Although the Discussion Draft codifies a refund program, the design

   Oncor’s Response to Commission Staff’s Second Request for Comments on P. 58484 at 3 (available at:
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/search/documents/?controlNumber=58484&itemNumber=42).
14

 of CIAC is not limited to customer-specific facilities and would require large loads to pay an undue
portion of grid costs that will be used to serve others.

       Notably, the Discussion Draft defines costs that are “directly attributable” to an
interconnecting customer to broadly include system costs that will be used to serve other
customers. Specifically, the language in Section (h)(9) references the costs associated with system
upgrades that would not exist “but for” the interconnecting large load customer. This standard
does not work. System upgrades are needed to serve total load—including the new customer and
all existing customers. Both the new customer and all existing customers are the “but for” cause
of the improvements. As a result, it is not clear how the Commission will identify when an
improvement would be needed “but for” the interconnecting large load. Importantly, transmission
system upgrades are needed for the totality of the customers served, and these upgrades are
typically not limited to one, single customer. For example, a 400 MW load may tip the scales to
justify the need for a new 345-kV line, but all existing load in the region is also a “but for” cause
of this upgrade as it is needed to serve the total load. Essentially, it would be just as accurate to
state that an improvement would not be needed “but for” a residential load that was included in
the forecast as well. This is particularly true in ERCOT’s postage-stamp transmission cost
allocation system where costs are shared among all customers under the belief that all customers
benefit from the enhanced transmission system.

       Additionally, it would be resource intensive, if not practically impossible, to actually
isolate the portion of a system upgrade actually caused by each specific customer. To do this, you
would need to determine what facilities would be needed anyway to serve other customers, as
compared to when the new large load is included. To try to isolate the costs caused by a large load
customer, ERCOT would need to continually re-run its Regional Transmission Planning (RTP)
analyses with and without each large load customer. The burden is further compounded when the
rule is implemented on a continuous basis and new large loads are added to the system.
Presumably the “but for” analysis is not static because the CIAC is recalculated based on new large
load customers. As a result, ERCOT would be forced to study the innumerable permutations of
when various load combinations were added to the system to try to isolate the costs of each upgrade
for each large load customers within the service area.




                                                  12
        Finally, due to the timing requirements, CIACs are estimates of facility costs. Today,
CIACs are ultimately trued-up based on the utility’s actual costs. This can result in an additional
charge to the customer if the utility under-estimated, or a refund if the utility over-estimated. For
clarity, the rule should specifically address this true-up process to ensure that customers are not
harmed or advantaged by inaccurate utility estimates.

       To address the issues outlined above, the Discussion Draft § (h)(9) should be amended as
follows:

   H. Utilities should retain flexibility in reallocating capacity from a large load customer
      if a milestone is missed.
       The Discussion Draft requires utilities to reallocate the capacity associated with a large
load customer if the customer fails to satisfy a load ramp milestone within 18 months. While TIEC
understands and agrees with the intent behind this requirement—ensuring the maximum utilization
of the system—mandating this treatment regardless of circumstances could be unnecessarily
restrictive and inefficient. Instead, the rule should give the utility the right to reallocate capacity
after 18 months if a milestone is missed, but also give the utilities flexibility to work with the
customer to update their ramp schedule if that makes more sense.

       There may be any number of reasons where a customer’s ramp is delayed, including forces
outside the customer’s control. It may not always be the most efficient solution to reallocate the
capacity and require a customer to essentially start over in the interconnection process for
additional capacity. Economic conditions can sometimes delay, rather than eliminate, a customer’s

requires the same capacity. Further, depending on the location, there may not be other customers
in need of that capacity. If the rule mandates strict reallocation after 18 months of a missed
milestone, both the utility and the customer may be forced to restart the entire process. This not
only adds unnecessary inefficiency but also creates additional burdens for all parties involved.

       To ensure flexibility and effective system management, the rule should allow utilities to
exercise discretion to determine whether reallocation is truly the best course of action based on
real-world circumstances. Utilities are naturally motivated to balance the interests of all customers
and will seek to interconnect as many customers as possible and to maximize use of their system.
As the primary point of contact, utilities are also best positioned to collaborate with customers and
assess the potential impacts of reallocating capacity. Rather than forcing utilities to reallocate
capacity within 18 months, the Commission should consider revising the language to give utilities
flexibility to work with large load customers who have missed a milestone. This would allow

                        IV.    RESPONSES TO STAFF’S QUESTIONS

1.     Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
       customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how
       should the commission define those parameters?
       Establishing clear parameters for determining when a large load customer is pursuing a
“substantially similar” interconnection request would benefit market participants by promoting
transparency and consistency in load forecasting. As a starting point, TIEC would suggest a
presumption that interconnection requests are “substantially similar” if: (i) they are requested by
the same entity, (ii) they are for the same approximate size (i.e., within a 10% MW range), and
(iii) the requested energization dates are within 24 months of each other. However, as noted
throughout these comments, certain types of businesses (such as oil and gas and midstream
businesses) will actually build numerous facilities with similar specifications each year. As a
result, a customer should be able to overcome this presumption by explaining whether the customer
intends to pursue several/all of the requests based on their business model. This approach would
at least open a dialogue with the customer when it appears that interconnection requests may be
duplicative.

2.     Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
       information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows
       a large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the
       commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not
       competitively sensitive information)? If so, what information should and should not
       be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and
       ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to
       materialize?
       The definition of “competitively sensitive information” must balance the objectives of
obtaining information for accurate forecasting against the need to protect the privacy and business
interests of large load customers. Under existing law, 16 TAC § 25.272(g) prohibits utilities from
disclosing any proprietary customer information, except under a few narrow circumstances.
Similarly, ERCOT is required to maintain the confidentiality of information submitted by TSPs
and transmission service customers that is designated as Protected Information under 16 TAC
§ 25.362(e), including proprietary customer information. For consistency with other rules and
general transparency, there could be language that clearly states that large load customer



                                                24
 disclosures are deemed to be confidential information (specifically, that they are “proprietary
customer information”) and are subject to the protections in the Commission’s rules.

        However, if these existing protections apply to disclosures under the rule (which TIEC
assumes is the case), then the scope of competitively sensitive information that is completely
withheld should be fairly narrow.

        For example, the Commission could consider defining “competitively sensitive
information” that can be completely withheld using the trade secret privilege standard. Under this
standard, the information must be more than merely what a competitor can use to its advantage.
The classic example of a “trade secret” is Colonel Sanders’ original blend of herbs and spices, or,
the Coca-Cola formula, where inadvertent disclosure would be so damaging that courts have
exempted the information from disclosure, even under a strict protective order. As the Texas
Supreme Court stated, “trade secret” is a term of art “that generally relates to the production of
goods, as, for example, a machine or formula for the production of an article.” 16 It does not include
general information related to business operations or financial data. 17 This approach would ensure
that only particularly damaging information would be completely exempt from the standard
disclosure requirements. If the disclosed information does not amount to a “trade secret,” it would
not qualify for anonymization or withholding under the Discussion Draft. All other competitively
sensitive and proprietary information would still need to be disclosed to ERCOT and the TSPs,
but it would be subject to existing protections for proprietary customer information as noted above.

based on current, accurate information about actual customer needs, protecting ratepayers and

                        EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   TIEC recommends removing the proposed language that would give ERCOT authority to
     impose operational requirements on large loads. It exceeds SB 6’s scope, lacks a legal
     basis under PURA, creates compliance burdens, and could deter economic development in
     Texas. Utilities have more expertise and are in a better position to impose technical
     requirements on customers than ERCOT.
 •   TIEC urges the Commission to revise the CIAC and financial security provisions so that
     large customers only pay for customer-dedicated facilities, not grid-wide upgrades that
     serve others. The current rule structure could deter economic development by placing
     undue cost burdens on large loads. TIEC recommends clearly distinguishing between costs
     for customer-specific facilities (CIAC) and broader system upgrades (financial security)
     based on potential facility use, and rejects the impractical “but for” standard for cost
     allocation. Additionally, TIEC requests the rule clarify the CIAC true-up process to ensure

                        IV.    RESPONSES TO STAFF'S QUESTIONS

1.     Should the commission define parameters for determining whether a large load
       customer is pursuing a substantially similar interconnection request? If so, how
       should the commission define those parameters?
       Establishing clear parameters for determining when a large load customer is pursuing a
"substantially similar" interconnection request would benefit market participants by promoting
transparency and consistency in load forecasting. As a starting point, TIEC would suggest a
presumption that interconnection requests are "substantially similar" if: (i) they are requested by
the same entity, (ii) they are for the same approximate size (i.e., within a 10% MW range), and
(iii) the requested energization dates are within 24 months of each other. However, as noted
throughout these comments, certain types of businesses (such as oil and gas and midstream
businesses) will actually build numerous facilities with similar specifications each year. As a
result, a customer should be able to overcome this presumption by explaining whether the customer
intends to pursue several/all of the requests based on their business model. This approach would
at least open a dialogue with the customer when it appears that interconnection requests may be
duplicative.

2.     Proposed subsections (c)(3), (e)(3), and (h)(3) require the disclosure of specific
       information related to a substantially similar request for interconnection and allows
       a large load customer to anonymize competitively sensitive details. Should the
       commission list what is and is not competitively sensitive (e.g., load zone is not
       competitively sensitive information)? If so, what information should and should not
       be considered competitively sensitive such that the interconnecting utility and
       ERCOT can identify whether there is a duplicate request, or a request is unlikely to
       materialize?
       The definition of "competitively sensitive information" must balance the objectives of
obtaining information for accurate forecasting against the need to protect the privacy and business
interests of large load customers. Under existing law, 16 TAC § 25.272(g) prohibits utilities from
disclosing any proprietary customer information, except under a few narrow circumstances.
Similarly, ERCOT is required to maintain the confidentiality of information submitted by TSPs
and transmission service customers that is designated as Protected Information under 16 TAC
§ 25.362(e), including proprietary customer information. For consistency with other rules and
general transparency, there could be language that clearly states that large load customer



                                                24
 disclosures are deemed to be confidential information (specifically, that they are "proprietary
customer information") and are subject to the protections in the Commission's rules.

         However, if these existing protections apply to disclosures under the rule (which TIEC
assumes is the case ), then the scope of competitively sensitive information that is completely
withheld should be fairly narrow.

         For example, the Commission could consider defining "competitively sensitive
information" that can be completely withheld using the trade secret privilege standard. Under this
standard, the information must be more than merely what a competitor can use to its advantage.
The classic example of a "trade secret" is Colonel Sanders' original blend of herbs and spices, or,
the Coca-Cola formula, where inadvertent disclosure would be so damaging that courts have
exempted the information from disclosure, even under a strict protective order. As the Texas
Supreme Court stated, "trade secret" is a term of art "that generally relates to the production of
goods, as, for example, a machine or formula for the production of an article." 16 It does not include
general information related to business operations or financial data. 17 This approach would ensure
that only particularly damaging information would be completely exempt from the standard
disclosure requirements. Ifthe disclosed information does not amount to a "trade secret," it would
not qualify for anonymization or withholding under the Discussion Draft. All other competitively
sensitive and proprietary information would still need to be disclosed to ERCOT and the TSPs,
but it would be subj ect to existing protections for proprietary customer information as noted above.

§25.194. Large Load Interconnection Standards.

      (a)    Purpose and Scope. This section sets forth the standards and criteria for an electric
             utility, including a municipally owned utility and electric cooperative, to
             interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission network.

      (b)    Definitions. The following words and terms, when used in this section, have the
             following meanings unless the context indicates otherwise:

             (1)    Backup generating facilities -- Generation facilities that are not capable of
                    exporting energy to the ERCOT transmission system and that, in aggregate,
                    can serve at least 50% of on-site contracted peak demand.

             (2)    Contracted peak demand -- the total peak demand that a large load
                    customer requests that an interconnecting electric utility serve at a site as
                    stated in an executed and securitized discretionary services agreement or
                    interconnection intefmedtate agreement.

             (3)     Discretionary services agreement -- An agreement, executed and
                    securitized by a large load customer and interconnecting electric utility after
                    the interconnecting electric utility completes the large load interconnection
                    study and before the interconnecting electric utility submits the study to
                    ERCOT, that, at a minimum, satisfies subsection of this section.

             (4)    End-use customer -- the legal entity that eventually will consume the
                    electricity for its operations at the site subj ect to an interconnection request
                    or a corporate affiliate seeking interconnection on behalf of such legal

      (5)     Interconnecting electric utility -- The electric utility, municipally owned
              utility, or electric cooperative that owns and operates the facilities necessary
              to interconnect a large load customer to the ERCOT transmission network.

              services agreement, intermediate agreement, or interconnection agreement,

           TEXAS INDUSTRIAL ENERGY CONSUMERS' COMMENTS
                        EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

 •   TIEC recommends removing the proposed language that would give ERCOT authority to
     impose operational requirements on large loads. It exceeds SB 6's scope, lacks a legal
     basis under PURA, creates compliance burdens, and could deter economic development in
     Texas. Utilities have more expertise and are in a better position to impose technical
     requirements on customers than ERCOT.
 •   TIEC urges the Commission to revise the CIAC and financial security provisions so that
     large customers only pay for customer-dedicated facilities, not grid-wide upgrades that
     serve others. The current rule structure could deter economic development by placing
     undue cost burdens on large loads. TIEC recommends clearly distinguishing between costs
     for customer-specific facilities (CIAC) and broader system upgrades (financial security)
     based on potential facility use, and rej ects the impractical "but for" standard for cost
     allocation. Additionally, TIEC requests the rule clarify the CIAC true-up process to ensure
     customers are charged based on actual facility costs.
 •   Following the intent of SB 6, the Discussion Draft should clarify that security requirements
     under a subsequent agreement will supersede prior agreements. The $/MW security
     amount under the DSA should count towards the security requirements under the
     intermediate agreement and/or FEA. If there are any excess security amounts because
     actual expected costs are less than the security, the security requirement should be reduced.
 •   If a project is withdrawn or canceled, any unused CIAC or financial security should be
     refunded after covering actual utility costs to prevent unnecessary penalties and support
     business flexibility.
 •   TIEC understands the need for disclosure requirements about whether the interconnection
     request is for a developer or end-use customer, but the definition of "end-use customer"
     should include entities seeking interconnection for a corporate affiliate.
 •   To avoid deterring economic activity, the $/MW security required under discretionary
     service agreements should be reduced from $50,000/MW to $20,000/MW. Additionally
     the security under the DSA should only apply to new, incremental capacity for expansions.
     Alternatively, the Commission could differentiate these amounts for "extra-large" loads,
     to avoid deterring industrial investment.
 •   If there is a long interconnection timeline, customers should be able to evaluate alternative
     sites without paying an additional study fee or to receive a refund of any unused amounts.
 •   Utilities should retain flexibility in reallocating capacity from a large load customer if a
     milestone is missed after it is energized.
